newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's new government still out for Pol Pot.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's new government still out for Pol Pot.

text.p: The new Cambodian government still wants to bring elusive Khmer Rouge guerrilla leader Pol Pot to an international court, a senior government official said on Wednesday.

First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh had been negotiating with a Khmer Rouge faction that broke with Pol Pot to secure his hand-over, but the bloody takeover and ouster of Ranariddh on July 6 brought those talks to an abrupt end.
But Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, who ousted Ranariddh, still wants to see Pol Pot and other senior Khmer Rogue leaders brought to justice.
"Government policy is the same. Pol Pot has to be brought to justice," Secretary of State for Information Khieu Kanharith told Reuters.

Hun Sen and Ranariddh agreed in late June that if Pol Pot was ever handed over to the government, he should be brought before an international court. Khieu Kanharith said that was still the view of the new government.

"According to international convention, you can bring people charged with war crimes either to a local or an international court. In the case of Cambodia, we believe an international court would be better," he said.
Pol Pot masterminded the 1975-79 "killing fields" regime, during which more than a million Cambodians died of starvation and disease, hard labour or were executed.

Khieu Kanharith said negotiations with lower-ranking members of the Khmer Rouge could be held, but the government would not accept any conditions on the talks. If talks failed the government might consider a military option, he said.
Political analysts in Phnom Penh said the secretive guerrilla group was most likely reassessing its position in the aftermath of Hun Sen's ouster of Ranariddh.
"I think they're probably feeling their way," one analyst said. "It always takes them time to form new policy and now they have to think again."
The guerrillas' clandestine radio, its main propaganda mouthpiece, has broadcast attacks on Hun Sen since his ouster of Ranariddh, condemning him as a mere "puppet" of Vietnam.

The radio, which is under the control of the guerrillas' political leader, Khieu Samphan, has also been saying that Pol Pot is politically finished. The radio has not said where Pol Pot was, but he is believed to be in the guerrillas' base at Anlong Veng in Cambodia's far north.

A government army officer under Hun Sen said on Tuesday that Khmer Rouge guerrillas were helping royalist forces in battles against government troops in northern Cambodia, although royalist leaders deny any military links with the Khmer Rouge.
Hun Sen and Ranariddh led an uneasy coalition government, but their relations turned hostile this year when Ranariddh announced he had opened peace talks with the Khmer Rouge.
Ranariddh said he was willing to form an alliance with Khieu Samphan, infuriating Hun Sen, who analysts said wanted to prevent any deal that would bolster his rival's position.

Hun Sen declared the prince's negotiations with the Khmer Rouge illegal, and justified his move against Ranariddh's forces on July 5 by saying Ranariddh's military commanders were bringing defectors from the guerrilla group into the capital.
The Khmer Rouge boycotted the 1993 election, saying the former Hanoi-backed government -- led by Hun Sen -- was not dismantled as stipulated in the Paris agreement.

In recent years, many rebels defected to the government. The hardcore remnants under Pol Pot, based at Anlong Veng, were riven by a violent split in June. Days later Pol Pot was denounced over Khmer Rouge radio and according to Ranariddh's negotiators, he was hunted down and captured by the Khieu Samphan faction.
